main_damage_causes: Loss of the Half-Blood Prince Apparition lesson arc showing Crabbe's growing resentment and mutinous exclusion from Malfoy's confidence, which was the essential psychological preparation for his Deathly Hallows rebellion

The climactic Room of Requirement sequence - Crabbe's only scene of genuine agency, independent speech, moral choice, and consequential action - is absent from the corpus, removing the sole moment where he transcends background henchman status

Systematic reduction of Crabbe to a silent visual presence (sleeping, slumbering, flanking) across multiple films, stripping the few book moments where he has individual comic physicality or reactive characterization, particularly the Shrieking Shack blundering scene and the Polyjuice comedy beats

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Polyjuice Potion preparation and execution (non-theatrical material lost)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Books establish Crabbe as a physically imposing but dim-witted follower who is tricked by drugged cakes, has his hair stolen, and is locked in a broom cupboard. The physical comedy of Ron impersonating Crabbe's lumbering gait, stiff arms, and low intelligence is a key characterization beat. Crabbe's obliviousness and greed are central to the scene working.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The scenes where Crabbe and Goyle are drugged, dragged, and locked away were cut from the theatrical release. The film retains the Polyjuice transformation and Slytherin common room interrogation but loses the direct physical characterization of Crabbe as a greedy, oblivious dupe. The real Crabbe never appears face-to-face with his doubles.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's characterization of Crabbe as comically greedy and oblivious (stuffing the drugged cake whole into his mouth, keeling over without changing expression) is a defining personality beat. Cutting this removes the only scene in Chamber of Secrets where Crabbe has any real comic presence independent of just flanking Malfoy.

damaging_scenes.scene: Prisoner of Azkaban - Great Hall feast, Malfoy feigning faint at dementor announcement (Film Scene 5)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Books establish Crabbe as a passive presence who follows Malfoy's lead and chortles along with whatever Malfoy does. The book does not describe this specific faint gag at the feast announcement.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus shows Draco flanked by Crabbe and Goyle at the Slytherin table as Malfoy feigns a dead faint at Dumbledore's dementor announcement. Crabbe is present but purely decorative, with no individual reaction described.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor: Crabbe is present but entirely backgrounded even in this moment of Slytherin group reaction. The books give Crabbe slightly more reactive presence (chortling, sniggering) but this is a small beat.

damaging_scenes.scene: Prisoner of Azkaban - Shrieking Shack encounter (Film Scene 9)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 176-181 establishes Crabbe and Goyle as physically intimidating but genuinely scared of invisible threats - 'their bulging muscles were no use against ghosts.' Crabbe blunders forward zombie-like with arms outstretched, gets pelted with mud, does a pirouette trying to find who threw a stick, and his foot accidentally catches Harry's cloak revealing him. This gives Crabbe a rare moment of comic physical individuality.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 9 shows Crabbe and Goyle advancing on Ron and Hermione when the invisible Harry pelts Malfoy with snowballs, then their knees give out and they fall headfirst into snow. They then run away with Malfoy. The blundering zombie-walk, the stick-throwing pirouette, and the accidental cloak-reveal are all absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book gives Crabbe his most individualized comic physical moment in the entire series - blundering forward with arms outstretched, doing a confused pirouette, inadvertently exposing Harry. The film reduces him to simply falling over and running. This strips one of the few scenes where Crabbe has any distinct comedic agency of his own rather than being a pure background presence.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Voldemort's graveyard resurrection (Film Scene 15)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 247-251 show Crabbe Senior among the Death Eaters called out by name at the graveyard resurrection. He bows clumsily and mutters 'We will, Master...' when Voldemort says he expects better from him. This establishes the Crabbe family as active, named Death Eaters - context critical for understanding Vincent Crabbe's later trajectory.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 15 shows Voldemort unmasking Death Eaters including 'Crabbe' by name, but Crabbe Senior is given no distinct dialogue or reaction shot - he is one of a group falling to their knees. The personal rebuke and the clumsiness noted in the book are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's graveyard scene establishes Crabbe Senior as a named, individually rebuked Death Eater who bows clumsily and mutters submission. This context directly informs why Vincent Crabbe would later be susceptible to Dark Arts radicalization (HBP/DH). The film names him but gives him no individual characterization, weakening the thematic through-line to his son's later turn.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Umbridge's office capture, Neville held in stranglehold (Film Scene 18 implied/Corpus Book Scene 334-336)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 334-336 show Crabbe holding Neville in a stranglehold that is genuinely dangerous - Neville is turning purple, nearly suffocating, and Snape orders 'Crabbe, loosen your hold a little. If Longbottom suffocates it will mean a lot of tedious paperwork.' This gives Crabbe genuine menace and a rare line of characterization.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus (Scene 18) shows the capture of Harry's friends but the specific detail of Crabbe strangling Neville and Snape's sardonic intervention is not present in the film corpus text. The scene exists in the film but Crabbe's dangerous grip on Neville and Snape's specific address to him is not evidenced in the corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book gives Crabbe one of his rare moments of individual menace and receives a direct line from Snape addressing him specifically. The film captures the capture scene generally but this specific beat - which gives Crabbe physical threat and individual address - is not evidenced in the film corpus, representing lost characterization.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Train compartment, Crabbe reading comic (Film Scenes 20-21)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 355-359 shows Crabbe sitting in the compartment reading a comic while Malfoy discusses his secret mission with cryptic hints. Crabbe and Goyle are described as 'sitting with their mouths open like gargoyles' when Malfoy hints at bigger things. Crabbe is shown as genuinely clueless about Malfoy's plans.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scenes 20-21 show Crabbe and Goyle slumbering in the compartment while Malfoy talks with Pansy and Zabini. Crabbe is asleep rather than awake and clueless. When Malfoy discusses his hints about leaving Hogwarts, the film corpus does not show Crabbe's gargoyle-mouthed bewilderment.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Small but indicative: in the book Crabbe is awake and clueless, visibly confused by Malfoy's cryptic statements. In the film he's simply asleep. The book beat - Crabbe being left in the dark about Malfoy's real mission even as his supposed best friend hints at it - is a minor characterization note that foreshadows their later falling-out in DH.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Apparition lesson, Crabbe arguing with Malfoy (Book Scene 384-385, film not evidenced)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 384-396 show Crabbe in open argument with Malfoy during the Apparition lesson, standing mutinously five feet away. Malfoy snaps at him 'Look, it's none of your business what I'm doing, Crabbe, you and Goyle just do as you're told and keep a lookout!' Crabbe is shown as increasingly resentful of being kept in the dark and treated as muscle. This is critical foreshadowing of his DH rebellion.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus does not contain any Apparition lesson scene or evidence of this argument between Crabbe and Malfoy. This entire arc of Crabbe's growing resentment at being excluded from Malfoy's confidence is absent from the film.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the most damaging single omission. The books show Crabbe's growing mutinous resentment at being treated as muscle while being kept ignorant of Malfoy's real mission - a through-line that directly explains his DH behavior where he openly defies Malfoy, declares 'I don't take your orders no more, Draco,' and recklessly uses Fiendfyre to assert dominance. Without this arc, his DH turn from loyal follower to dangerously independent rebel appears unmotivated. The film loses the entire psychological preparation for Crabbe's death scene.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows - Room of Requirement, Crabbe's rebellion and death (Book Scenes 415-457, not in film corpus)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 419-457 give Crabbe his most substantial characterization in the entire series. He speaks his first real lines ('We 'ung back, Potter. We decided not to go. Decided to bring you to 'im' - in a surprisingly soft voice), openly defies Malfoy ('I don't take your orders no more, Draco. You an' your dad are finished'), twice casts Avada Kedavra, recklessly unleashes Fiendfyre he cannot control, and dies as a result. He is described as speaking 'like a small child promised a large bag of sweets' - a complex mix of menace and arrested development. He calls Harry 'scum' and taunts 'Like it hot?'. His death is noted as tragic by Malfoy ('C-Crabbe... He's dead').
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus provided does not contain the Deathly Hallows Room of Requirement scene. This is the climactic scene of Crabbe's entire character arc in the books.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Room of Requirement sequence is Crabbe's defining moment in the entire saga. It is the only time he speaks at length, acts independently, makes his own choices (both the decision to hang back from Voldemort's gathering and the catastrophic decision to use Fiendfyre), openly rebels against Malfoy, and meets his end. His death closes the arc of the Malfoy trio and is the direct consequence of his radicalization by the Carrows. The film's handling of this (using Blaise Zabini in place of Crabbe due to Jamie Waylett's legal issues) means the entire culmination of Crabbe's book characterization is absent. This is not evidenced in the provided corpus but is the single largest structural damage to the character.
